newsitem.title: EGYPT: Libyan pretender slams Gaddafi bomb probe motive. [CORRECTED 13:10 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Libyan pretender slams Gaddafi bomb probe motive. [CORRECTED 13:10 GMT]

text.p: The pretender to the Libyan throne said on Wednesday (Corrects from Tuesday) Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi had agreed to let French investigators put four key intelligence and justice officials on trial because he wants to get rid of them.

Prince Mohammed al-Hassan al-Senoussi, the exiled nephew of the last king of Libya, told Reuters from his home in London there was a deep rift between Gaddafi and several of his closest aides and that using them as scapegoats for the bombing of a French airliner in 1989 was a sure way to isolate them.
"They're certainly scapegoats because Gaddafi is the only one who gave the orders for this bombing," Senoussi said.

"By giving them up for trial, he's killing two birds with one stone -- getting them out of the country because he's become very suspicious of them and also turning the accusing fingers away from himself."

Earlier this month, Gaddafi allowed France's chief anti-terrorism investigator Jean-Louis Bruguiere into Libya to gather information about the bombing of the UTA airlines DC-10 over the Sahara. All 170 passengers and crew died in the crash.
The bombing occurred at the height of tension between France and Libya over Chad, where forces from the two countries clashed repeatedly in the 1970s and 1980s.

Libya has so far refused to turn over any of the suspects although the U.N. has slapped tough economic sanctions on Tripoli to encourage its cooperation in the probe into the 1989 UTA crash and that of the Pan Am flight over Scotland in 1988.
Bruguiere wants six Libyans -- including Gaddafi's brother-in-law and two secret service agents -- to be tried in absentia next year.
"Gaddafi knows he cannot just kill all these men, they are of his tribe, so he's found a convenient way to replace them by new faces which will be totally loyal to him," Senoussi said.

The Libyan leader has recently launched a nationwide "purification" campaign against corruption and racketeering which opposition sources say is just a front to get rid of powerful and increasingly disgruntled cohorts.
Senoussi said the disparity between France's suspect list and the victims of Gaddafi's secret plot was proof the Libyan leader had ulterior motives for cooperating.

He listed four names which Gaddafi was targetting: the leader's brother-in-law Abdallah el-Senoussi, deputy head of intelligence, Moussa Mohammed Koussa of the internal communications committee, Hamad Hegazi from the justice ministry and Ibrahim el-Beshari, who is in charge of external security.
Apart from Abdallah el-Senoussi, France wants alleged secret agents Abdesslam Issa Shibani, Abdesslam Hamouda, Ibrahim Naeli and Musbah Arbas. It also issued a warrant for diplomat Abdallah Elazragh.
